newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline prices up sharply amid tight stocks.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline prices up sharply amid tight stocks.

text.p: Gasoline prices rose sharply on Friday, boosted by strong demand, tightening supplies and the rising price of a key gasoline blending component.

"We have tight supplies of RFG (reformulated gaosline) in the New York Harbor and tight supplies of MTBE (methyl butyl tertiary ether) which you need to make RFG, and that is forcing refiners to go out there and buy the August month," said Jim Fiedler, trader with E. D. & F. Man International in New York.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline for August delivery settled 1.82 cents higher at 64.03 cents a gallon.
Gasoline's rally swept the rest of the oil complex higher, with September crude settling 12 cents higher at $19.89 a barrel and August heating oil finishing 0.60 cent a gallon up at 53.99 cents.
Gasoline's strength is coming late in the summer and follows lofty implied demand which has averaged 8.7 million barrels per day, according to data from the American Petroleum Institute.

Meanwhile, production of MTBE has been disrupted over the past couple of months, making the component expensive. MTBE is a blending component for refomrulated gasoline, the grade deliverable against the futures contract.
Commercial players have been noted buyers throughout the week, and dealers said U.S. Gulf refiners were buying on Friday.

Traders have linked part of the buying to the maintenance shutdown of Tosco Corp.'s crude unit at its Bayway refinery in New Jersey. The crude unit supplies feedstock to a large gasoline-making unit there.
Moreover, on Thursday, a source familiar with Coastal Corp.'s Aruba refinery said the 210,000 bpd plant will undergo major maintenance in September.
The Aruba plant, Coastal's largest, is a major supplier of feedstocks for gasoline-making units in the U.S. Gulf and Caribbean region.
Dealers questioned how much longer August gasoline's strength would last, however, in light of the contract's expiration next Thursday and the possible resumption of Iraqi oil sales in August.

United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan is expected to meet U.N. officials this weekend to discuss a food distribution plan submitted by Iraq Monday. The U.N. review was expected to be completed by the end of July.
Devising the plan has delayed the next three months of the "oil-for-food" accord under which the U.N. has allowed Iraq to sell oil in exchange for humanitarian aid.
"It's hard to pinpoint a top to this market. One has to know when there will be Iraqi crude and how much," said E .D. F. Man's Fiedler.
Copper prices rose sharply on heavy fund shortcovering, aided by strength in the other base metals, particularly zinc and nickel.
At New York's Commodity Exchange, copper for September delivery closed at 111.45 cents a lb, up 3.65 cents.
Funds were believed to have amassed short positions over the last month, forcing the active September contract down from a high of 123.60 cents a lb on June 20 to a low of 104.00 cents on July 9.
"The funds have been short all month," said David Rinehimer, director of futures research at Smith Barney. "It feels like an overdue correction in a bear market."

The market took its cue from the zinc and nickel markets in London, he said. The zinc market is currently in the throes of a squeeze in which prices are lodged at seven-year highs. Nickel is at its highest price in a month on strike fears at Falconbridge's Sudbury mine.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange lumber prices were stronger, supported by news that British Columbia's coastal forest companies had canceled contract talks with the lumber workers' union, dealers said.
The move came after wildcat strikes at International Forest Products Ltd.
Dealers said, however, that the short-term impact should be minor with supplies of prompt wood currently plentiful.
"There is enough inventory at mills and a secondary level to sustain us unless is it a long strike," one dealer said.
Lumber for September delivery closed up $1.10 at $346.60 per thousand board feet.
